name: Orvana Occasion Gown — Tail-Vent Standard
description:
Orvana's accessible line — distinct from their Spire couture — is designed for Tier 3 buyers who want genuine tailoring at a price that doesn't require financing. The Occasion Gown is floor-length, cut in a silk-analog that holds color well and resists static cling in the charged air of most Meridian indoor venues. The Tail-Vent Standard variant includes a structured rear panel that splits cleanly from mid-hip to hem, with internal tension bands that keep the split closed when standing and open naturally under movement. It accommodates most TESSERA standard-issue geneware tails without bunching or binding.

Orvana offers the gown in twelve colorways and four standard geneware configurations: tail-vent, wing-slit back, horn-clearance hood attachment, and standard. Custom configurations are available for an additional Φ40–Φ80. The construction is clean and the fit is reliable. It is not a statement piece — it is a dress that works, that lasts, and that doesn't make the wearer think about it during the event.
cultural_context: The Orvana Occasion line is the default formal purchase for Tier 3 geneware-modified individuals. It's common enough at mid-tier events that it reads as baseline rather than aspirational. Some people are proud of it; others find it slightly embarrassing to be wearing the same gown as three other people at the same function. Orvana has responded to this by expanding their colorway range annually.
story_hooks: At a corporate reception, the character is wearing the same gown in the same colorway as a TESSERA genomics consultant. The consultant assumes this means they work for TESSERA. The character doesn't correct her immediately.

The character's tail is a non-standard TESSERA modification — slightly longer and heavier than the spec the Tail-Vent Standard is designed for. The tension bands give out midway through an important event.

A fashion journalist from a Ringo lifestyle feed is doing a piece on 'the democratization of geneware fashion.' They want to photograph the character in the gown. The character has complicated feelings about being used as evidence of progress.
